title: Why You Need the Same Pieces

steps.body: Fractions add by counting pieces — but only when the pieces are the same size. Halves and thirds cannot be counted together any more than metres and inches can.
steps.narration: Fractions add by counting pieces — but only when the pieces are the same size. Halves and thirds cannot be counted together any more than metres and inches can.

widget.prompt: Rename 1/2 as sixths so it can meet 1/3.
widget.successFeedback: 3/6 — the same amount as 1/2, now cut into pieces that thirds can be counted with.
widget.lowFeedback: That build is SHORTER than 3/6 — either shade more pieces or make each piece larger until the lengths match.
widget.highFeedback: That build is LONGER than 3/6 — either shade fewer pieces or make each piece smaller until the lengths match.

commonFractions.feedback: 1/6 is one sixth-piece; a half needs three of them to hold the same amount.
2/5 is what adding across gives, and it is smaller than the 1/2 you started with.

predict.prompt: Can 1/2 and 1/3 be added by counting, as they stand?
predict.reveal: A half and a third are different-sized pieces, so there is nothing common to count until both are renamed.

cml.actionGoal: Rename both fractions to the same piece size, then count the pieces for g5u why common.
invariants: Fractions add and subtract only when their pieces are the same size: renaming scales both parts of a fraction and leaves its value untouched, which is what makes g5u why common a counting problem once the denominators agree.
misconceptions: Adding numerators and denominators across, scaling only one part of a fraction when renaming, or forgetting to trade a whole when the top fraction is too small to subtract from.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If only the numerators were made equal instead of the denominators, what would go wrong?

widget.prompt: Why can 1/2 + 1/3 not be added by adding the tops and the bottoms?

options.label: Because halves and thirds are different-sized pieces
options.feedback: Correct — adding counts only works when every piece is the same size, which is what renaming achieves.

options.label: Because 2/5 is too small to be right
options.feedback: The answer being wrong is the symptom; the cause is that the pieces were never made the same size.

options.label: Because you must always simplify first
options.feedback: 1/2 and 1/3 are already in lowest terms; simplifying changes nothing here.

options.label: You can — 2/5 is correct
options.feedback: 1/2 alone is already more than 2/5, so a sum that lands below one of its parts cannot be right.

That subtracted the denominators. Renaming SCALES both parts; it never subtracts.
